title: Epicurus on Fearing Death
objective: After this level you can explain Epicurus's argument that death is nothing to us, and weigh the reply that death harms us by taking away future goods.
summary: Epicurus argued that death is nothing to us because good and bad need sensation; Lucretius compared the time after death to the time before birth; Nagel replied that death deprives us of life’s goods.

cards.headline: Should you fear something you will never experience?
cards.body: Epicurus thought the fear of death rests on a mistake, and he offered an argument to cure it. Philosophers have been testing that argument ever since.

cards.headline: Where death is, you are not
cards.body: In his Letter to Menoeceus, Epicurus reasons in two steps. Good and bad require sensation, and death is the end of all sensation. So death is nothing to us, “seeing that, when we are, death is not come, and, when death is come, we are not.” Nothing can be bad for you if there is no you left to feel it.

cards.headline: The mirror behind you
cards.body: His follower Lucretius added a picture. Look back at the endless time before you were born. It never troubled you. Nature, he says, holds that time up like a mirror of the time after we are gone. If the first stretch of nothing holds nothing to fear, why fear the second?

cards.headline: What death takes away
cards.body: Thomas Nagel replied in his essay “Death” (1970). Something can be bad for you without being felt, if it takes away good things. Sleep through a celebration you’d longed for and you feel no pain, yet you lost something. Death, he argued, is bad in that way: it deprives you of the goods more life would have held.

cards.headline: Epicurus on Fearing Death: the big picture
learned: Epicurus: good and bad need sensation
So death is nothing to us
Lucretius: the mirror of the time before birth
Nagel: death takes away future goods

questions.prompt: Why did Epicurus say that death is nothing to us?

options.label: The soul lives on in another world after death
options.rationale: Epicurus argued from the end of sensation.

options.label: When we exist death is absent, and when it comes we are gone
Death is always painless
options.rationale: His point is about being dead, not dying.

options.label: The gods protect good people from a painful death
options.rationale: He doesn’t appeal to the gods here.

questions.explanation: Good and bad need sensation, and death ends sensation: when we are, death is not, and when death is, we are not.

questions.prompt: Match each thinker with his idea about death.
questions.explanation: Epicurus argued in his Letter to Menoeceus, Lucretius said the time before birth is held up like a mirror, and Nagel argued death deprives you of the goods more life would have held.

questions.prompt: Epicurus’s case is an argument in Level 1’s sense: premises supporting a conclusion. Which of these is one of its premises?

options.label: Death is the worst of all evils
options.rationale: That’s the fear he argues against.

options.label: Everyone fears death equally
options.rationale: His argument doesn’t rest on this.

questions.explanation: An argument gives reasons, called premises, for a conclusion. Epicurus’s premises: good and bad need sensation, and death ends it. Conclusion: death is nothing to us.
